# Request: positive control for the Q-based misfit test, and an SE-ratio summary

Context: my review of the Outline rev 9 (`story-repo`, issue linked in my comment there) asks whether Δ(log Q) against the same-graph null can detect a misfit at all. 1. **Positive control.** One synthetic experiment on the Arena-55k graph (and ideally on a 6-model complete graph): simulate from the fitted BT with a known departure (question/annotator random effect that adds overdispersion; a position-bias term; a cyclic/intransitive component), at two or three sizes, and compute Δ(log Q) for delete and flip with the same rule (z_fisher in [1,8], own null, interval over models, margin 0.15). Report the departure size at which the interval leaves ±0.15. Either outcome is a result: "the test detects overdispersion of size X" or "Q is insensitive to these departures".
2. **SE ratio per data set.** `se_gap_cmp_boot` / `se_model_based` and the cluster-bootstrap `se_gap` / `se_model_based`, median over the pairs in the declared range, for each real data set and for its null replicates. issue.author: idea-review-repo
issue.body:
# Review of PREANALYSIS.md (experiment-repo b82e575) — the analysis plan's decision rules

From `idea-review-repo`, read-only on your repository, as a plan review (the Outline's §3a defers these margins to your note). I read the note, not the scripts. The calibration work is good: the correction of P_flip(f) = Φ(−z√((1−f)/f)) and the finding that Q is not ≥ 1 under exact refit are exactly the kind of thing the note is for, and the timing disclosure (note written after looking at MT-Bench and ~28 Arena pairs, margins from synthetic data only) must go into the paper's reproduction notes as written. Points, most important first.

**1. C2's rule is close to automatic inside the declared range.** Random deletion of f ≤ 0.5 has P_flip ≈ Φ(−z√((1−f)/f)) ≤ Φ(−z), so for z in [1,8] a random process almost never reaches q = 16% (only z ≈ 1 does). Then ρ_q is nearly always a lower bound ">", and "far below noise (ρ ≥ 3)" is satisfied by construction, not by the data. Make the primary C2 statistic one that is defined for every pair: the **equal-budget comparison** — P_flip of random deletion/flip at budget k* (and at 0.5k*, 2k*), against the adversary's success probability of 1 at k* — together with F = k*·g_max/SE (the adversary's size in noise-SE units; random change has expected size ≈ 1 SE at the matching fraction). Keep ρ_q only where random reaches q, and report the share of pairs where it does.

**2. C4's "Δ ≈ 0" is not an equivalence test.** "|Δ| < 0.10 and the interval includes 0" lets a wide interval claim equivalence. Require the whole interval to lie within (−0.10, 0.10) (the TOST logic), and say what is written when |Δ| < 0.10 but the interval is wider ("not distinguishable from 0 or from ±0.10 at this size"). Also check that 0.10 is above the instance-level spread you found in the null (sd of mean log Q = 0.06 per configuration): a margin of 1.7 sd is thin for a three-way decision; consider 0.15 or justify. Jackknife over models with M = 6 (MT-Bench) has 6 units; say its interval is coarse there and report it as such.

**3. C1 compares against a pooled null; the null is graph-dependent.** Your own calibration shows null Q varies 0.90–1.35 by family, density and ties. "Median Q_real within 1.25 of the pooled-null median across datasets" can then fail or pass for graph reasons alone. Compare each dataset with *its own* null (same graph, counts, tie rate) for the collapse statement, and keep the pooled comparison only as a descriptive panel. The slope bands (z: [0.95, 1.28], N: [0.28, 0.60]) are fine, but note that the empirical N slope (0.43–0.45) is not the 0.5 the Brief's theory gives; the paper should state the empirical exponent and not "k* ∝ z√N" as a result.

**4. C5 cannot estimate a design term for most held-out datasets.** Crowd (Arena-55k) and expert (MT-Bench human) are single datasets: with leave-one-dataset-out, the held-out design level is absent from training, so a design coefficient is not defined there. A design term can only be tested where the design has ≥ 2 units (LLM-judge: the judges; sports: seasons; crowd: 55k vs 140k and slices). Say so in the rule. Also "RMSE drops by > 0.05" with a residual sd of 0.2–0.23 and few units is within noise; use a paired comparison over held-out units (difference in held-out squared error with a bootstrap/sign interval across units) and report the number of units, as the rule already requires.

**5. The "search is tight" evidence is for tiny problems.** 53 problems with M = 3–4, N = 30–70 and the MT-Bench anchor do not show tightness at Arena scale (M ≈ 60+, 2016 pairs, k* in the hundreds or more). Add a scale check that does not need a certificate: for a sample of Arena pairs, run an independent, stronger search (randomised restarts, swap/local search, or the Frank-Wolfe with several initialisations at a larger budget) and report the distribution of k*_improved / k*_standard; and plant instances (extend an observed dataset with an alteration set of known size that flips a pair, using the BT fit's own fitted counts) to see whether the search recovers the planted size or less. Where only the "lower-bound candidate" exists (Nelder–Mead over θ*), keep it labelled as a candidate in every table, and state that the LP is exact only for fixed θ*, so the sandwich is a certificate only on the small anchors.

**6. B = 100 for the matched-contrast joint bootstrap is coarse.** A 95% percentile interval from 100 draws rests on ~3 tail points and cannot reliably decide "excludes 0" near the margin 0.10. Use B ≥ 300–500 for the few headline matched contrasts (restrict to the z-strata of the main figure if the cost of re-running the search per replicate is the constraint), or use the bootstrap SE with a normal interval and say so. For the null, R = 20 replicates × 300 pairs is fine as the null's spread, but report the per-dataset null spread next to Δ.

**7. C3 definition.** "Non-overlapping model CIs" (Arena's published view) and "pair-gap CI excludes 0" are not the same set (BT scores are correlated through the gauge, so overlap of marginal CIs is conservative). Report the headline for one stated definition and the other as a sensitivity check; the published-view version is the one a reader recognises.

**8. Consistency with the Outline.** The Outline's rev 2 (per `story-repo`#3) proposes defaults (±0.15 slope band, factor 1.5, δ ≥ log 1.25, 1.2 for search tightness, log 2 for held-out error) that differ from this note (1.25, 0.10, 1.05, 0.05, ...). The pre-analysis note should be the single source: tell `story-repo` which numbers are in force so the Outline cites the note instead of repeating different values.

Nothing here asks you to restart runs. Points 1, 2, 3 and 4 change only how the results are summarised and can be done on the stored per-pair results; point 5 is an additional (small) experiment; point 6 is a setting. If you reject a point, say so here with the reason; I review again if the note changes.

issue.body:
# 研究任务：成对比较排行榜的稳定性

## 问题与动机

许多公开的模型评测排行榜（例如基于用户投票的大模型竞技场）通过聚合大量
「A 与 B 比较，谁更好」的成对偏好数据，用 Bradley-Terry 等成对比较模型拟合
每个参赛者的分数，再据此给出排名与置信区间。这些排名常被用于选型、发布宣传和
研究比较，但它们对底层比较数据的依赖程度并不清楚。

本任务研究：这类排行榜的排名对底层比较数据的小幅改动有多敏感（改动可能来自数据噪声，也可能来自
有人有意为之），以及这种敏感性在不同数据集、不同评测设计（例如众包投票、专家标注、模型裁判、
体育比赛）之间是否不同。

## 要求与证据标准

请自行界定可操作的研究问题，选择数据集和评价指标，设计并实现分析方法，用实验给出有证据支持的
结论。方法路线与对比基线由你自选。结论应基于至少两类不同评测设计的真实数据；改动的规模如何
度量、不同数据集之间如何比较，由你定义并说明理由。结论须说明适用条件与局限，而不只是给出单一
数字；"敏感性很小""视条件而定""与预期不同"同样是可以接受的结论。

## 约束

仅用 CPU、时间约一周、使用公开数据（见 `data.md`、`resources.md`）；产出为一篇研究论文及复现
代码（见 `deliverable.md`）。

# 研究任务：成对比较排行榜的稳定性

## 问题与动机

许多公开的模型评测排行榜（例如基于用户投票的大模型竞技场）通过聚合大量
「A 与 B 比较，谁更好」的成对偏好数据，用 Bradley-Terry 等成对比较模型拟合
每个参赛者的分数，再据此给出排名与置信区间。这些排名常被用于选型、发布宣传和
研究比较，但它们对底层比较数据的依赖程度并不清楚。

本任务研究：这类排行榜的排名对底层比较数据的小幅改动有多敏感（改动可能来自数据噪声，也可能来自
有人有意为之），以及这种敏感性在不同数据集、不同评测设计（例如众包投票、专家标注、模型裁判、
体育比赛）之间是否不同。

## 要求与证据标准

请自行界定可操作的研究问题，选择数据集和评价指标，设计并实现分析方法，用实验给出有证据支持的
结论。方法路线与对比基线由你自选。结论应基于至少两类不同评测设计的真实数据；改动的规模如何
度量、不同数据集之间如何比较，由你定义并说明理由。结论须说明适用条件与局限，而不只是给出单一
数字；"敏感性很小""视条件而定""与预期不同"同样是可以接受的结论。

## 约束

仅用 CPU、时间约一周、使用公开数据（见 `data.md`、`resources.md`）；产出为一篇研究论文及复现
代码（见 `deliverable.md`）。

issue.author: idea-review-repo
issue.body:
# Review of the Brief (revision of 2026-11-26 03:46) and prior_work.md — request for a response

Overall: a strong, well-scoped idea. Strong points first, then what to fix (ordered by how much each would cost the paper at review), then what would make it stronger. Nothing below asks you to narrow the study.

## Strong
- The question is operational and each conclusion type (C1–C4) is something a reader actually takes from a leaderboard.
- The two matched contrasts (same Arena battles: crowd vs LLM judges; same MT-Bench items: expert vs GPT-4) are the best asset: they isolate the label process from the comparison graph. NBA's 70 seasons give a distribution, not one number.
- "k* is an upper bound, verified by exact refit", first-order vs exact validation, and the synthetic-BT check are the right rigour.
- Every outcome ("small", "depends", "unexpected") is stated as publishable, which matches the objective.

## Must fix (each would be a reviewer's first objection)

**1. The noise scale A(C) = eps_50^random / (k*/N) is probably undefined.** Random flips/deletions are mean-preserving in direction. Random outcome-flips at rate eps shrink BT scores toward 0 but do not reorder a pair whose true gap has the sign of the fitted gap; random deletion of a fraction f gives a flip probability about Φ(−z·√(1−f)), which is always < 1/2. So "the random change that flips C half the time" does not exist except in degenerate limits (eps→0.5, f→1), and where it exists it measures something other than noise. Define the noise yardstick differently, e.g. (a) the bootstrap/subsample flip probability P_flip(C) at the actual N, and (b) a *noise-equivalent count*: the number of comparisons whose worst-case alteration moves the gap by 1 bootstrap SE, i.e. k*(C) expressed in units of SE (k*·g_max/SE, with g_max the largest per-comparison influence on the gap), or the f at which P_flip first reaches a stated level (5%, 16%). Say in the paper why the chosen scale is the natural one and test that it behaves on the synthetic-BT data.

**2. k*/N is not comparable across datasets of different N, by construction.** With gap Δ = z·SE and SE ∝ 1/√N, theory gives k* ≈ Δ/g_max ∝ z·√N, so k*/N ∝ z/√N: a dataset with 10× the votes looks ~3× more "robust" in fraction of N for the same statistical separation. The brief mentions matching and fragility-vs-N curves, but the headline definitions (H3 thresholds of 0.5/1/2% of N; "orders of magnitude differ across datasets") inherit the N effect. State the expected scaling up front, make the normalised quantity (e.g. k*/(z·√N) or k* in SE units) the cross-dataset currency, and make thresholds in H3 either per-√N or per-SE, not per-N. Use equal-N subsampling for every cross-design comparison, as you already plan, but as the primary result rather than a robustness check.

**3. The design effect (H2) is not identifiable as stated.** The observations are conclusions (pairs) within datasets, and there is one dataset per design except sports: crowd = Arena-55k (+140k), expert = MT-Bench human, LLM judge = potsawee + MT-Bench GPT-4, sports = NBA. "Design" is confounded with "dataset", and conclusions in one dataset share a graph and votes, so a cluster bootstrap over pairs gives no honest uncertainty on a design factor with ~4 levels. Be explicit about what carries the design claim: (i) the two matched contrasts (within-graph paired differences, with uncertainty from resampling battles/questions); (ii) the multiple judges inside potsawee as replicates of the LLM-judge design; (iii) NBA seasons as replicates of the sports design; (iv) Arena-140k vs 55k and, if feasible, category/language/time slices of 140k as replicates inside crowd. Say in the paper that the design factor is estimated from these, and that inference about "crowd vs expert" in general is limited to the instances studied.

**4. The search-quality confound.** Reported k* is an upper bound from a heuristic search whose tightness may differ by design (sparse small graphs, ties, heavy-tailed influence, nonlinearity near the optimum). A gap in k*/N between designs could be a gap in search quality. Report per dataset the gap between first-order prediction and exact refit, and use it as a covariate or sensitivity analysis in H2. Where exactness is reachable (MT-Bench: 6 models, 15 pairs; subsampled problems), compute exact or near-exact minima (small ILP/branch-and-bound or an exhaustive check on subsets) as an anchor, ideally also a *lower* bound (e.g. a relaxed/linear certificate) so the sandwich k*_lower ≤ k* ≤ k*_upper is reported.

**5. The novelty claim must not rest on being first.** Starter item 8 (Huang et al. 2025) is on the list and by the objective's wording is probably close to the published paper; you did not read it, which is the safe choice and I agree with it. But "No existing study we know of …" is then unverified at exactly the point where a reviewer will check. Phrase contributions as what this study adds that holds regardless: the noise–intent common scale, the design-vs-statistics separation (matched designs + parametric-bootstrap null, see below), the search-vs-exact gap, and CI-separated ≠ robust quantified per design. Make "to our knowledge, among the sources we could consult" the wording, and keep "dropping a few votes flips the top model" as a replication-type observation, not the headline. Keep the rule on the two April-2026 preprints: do not read them unless someone first rules out the forbidden-paper conflict; I suggest not reading them at all (they are not needed for the study).

## Fix / specify (smaller, but each is a place the plan could silently go wrong)

6. **Perturbation realism per family.** Deletion is not an action anyone can take on crowd votes: it measures data dependence (AMIP), not intent. Flip and insertion are adversarial but with different threat models. Min et al. inserters must go through the sampler (cannot choose opponent freely), whereas "add k votes for target vs competitor" assumes free choice. State the threat model per family, which of "noise" or "intent" each corresponds to, and count cost per unit consistently (a flip of a win = 1 alteration; flip of a tie = ?; deletion = 1; insertion = 1). Compare insertion with Min et al.'s strategies only under a matched threat model, otherwise as a lower-bound-on-cost anchor.
7. **Use more than adjacent pairs.** Adjacent and top-1/2 pairs are mostly in the noise (tiny z) and sit in a narrow z range. For H2/H3 you need a dose–response in z-gap: sample pairs stratified by z-gap from the whole model set (Arena has thousands of pairs), plus the standard leaderboard views (rank by CI as Arena publishes it: rank = 1 + number of models with CI-above). Otherwise the regression of log k* on covariates has little leverage.
8. **A parametric-bootstrap null makes the design effect operational.** Generate data from each dataset's fitted BT (same graph, same counts, same fitted scores, tie rate) and compute k* on it, labelled synthetic. Real − synthetic is the fragility due to *misfit* (position/length bias, intransitivity, non-stationarity, heterogeneous voters), separate from separation and density. Bootstrap by the correct cluster (question/battle), not by comparison, or the SEs and P_flip are too small. For matched contrasts, resample battles jointly in both labelings.

MT-Bench human data have two turns and ties: fix treatment in advance.
11. **Estimator scope vs a one-week CPU budget.** Six estimators × four conclusion types × three perturbation families × four+ datasets × bootstrap-over-search is too much to do evenly. State a priority order: the core cell is BT-MLE (ties as half wins) × {C1, C2} × {deletion, flip} on all datasets; the rest (Rao–Kupper/Davidson, ridge, Elo, win-rate, Rank Centrality, insertion, C3, C4) are extensions in a stated order, so a clipped budget delivers a complete core, not partial everything. Add Min et al.'s threat model to the positioning, and cite the top-K identifiability theory (Chen et al. 2019) where the √N scaling above is used, since that is where it earns its place.

- A small **predictive result**: a one-line rule (k* from z-gap, N and graph density, tested out of sample across datasets) is the thing readers will use; it also demonstrates whether "design" adds anything (H2).

comments.body:
Review 2 (Brief revision 2): the response is thorough and I accept it as adopting review 1; the structure now holds. Three corrections remain, the first a mathematical slip.

1. **"Q = F/z is 1 under linear theory" is wrong.** In the linear (first-order) problem the optimal k* is the smallest k whose k largest per-comparison influences sum to the gap, so k*·g_max ≥ gap, hence F ≥ z and Q ≥ 1, with equality only if all influences equal g_max. Q > 1 therefore arises from the *shape of the influence distribution* (a light tail ⇒ Q ≈ 1, a heavy tail ⇒ larger Q) even with a perfectly well-specified BT model; the exact nonlinear k* can push Q below its linear value. So Q alone cannot be read as "adversarial efficiency" or "misfit". Fix: state Q ≥ 1 in the linear regime, say that its baseline depends on the influence distribution, and take the reference from the parametric-bootstrap null (Q_real vs Q_null on the same graph, counts and fitted scores), as H2 already does. Alternatively replace g_max by a defined effective influence (e.g. mean of the top-k influences, or the gap divided by the sum of the top-k) so that the linear baseline is exactly 1 by construction. Either way, check on the synthetic data before the quantity is named in the paper.
2. **f_16% / f_5% have a limited range.** With P_flip(f) ≈ Φ(−z√(1−f)), f_16% = 1 − 1/z² exists only for z > 1, and for z = 4–5 it asks for 94–96% of the data deleted (an extrapolation beyond anything observed). For z < 1 the flip probability already exceeds 16% at f = 0. Report the whole P_flip(f) curve and use f_q only inside the range where it is inside (0, ~0.8); state the z-range in which the intent-vs-noise comparison is made, and do not average over pairs outside it.
3. **H4 held-out unit.** With ~6 datasets (plus NBA seasons) the out-of-sample test is leave-one-dataset-out (or leave-one-design-out), not leave-pairs-out; pairs from the same graph are not independent held-out units. Say so, report the number of effective held-out units, and treat a "design term improves held-out prediction" result as limited to those instances. NBA seasons allow a larger number of held-out units for the sports design only.

Minor: z uses the cluster-bootstrap SE; say which SE enters F (model-based Fisher or cluster-bootstrap), since F/z then differs by the design effect of clustering. Nothing else outstanding; no new review is needed until the Brief changes again or the Outline appears.

# Review of Outline rev 9 (§3b, results taken in): four points; the first matters most

I read §3b against the rules in `PREANALYSIS.md` rev 2 and the result schema (`fragility_conclusions.csv` has `z`, `z_fisher`, `se_gap`, `se_model_based`, `se_gap_cmp_boot`, `k_first_order`, `k_null_mean`, so most of what is asked below is already computed). I did not recompute any number.

**1. "No design-specific misfit detected" (C4) rests on a statistic with probably little power to detect misfit.**
Q = k\*·g_max/gap is pinned near 1 by the first-order identity: across the synthetic grid it moves only between 0.97 and 1.35, and the null's own spread is 0.06 on log scale. A real data set whose comparisons carry position bias, annotator or question clustering, or intransitive cycles has a different residual structure, but the count of alterations needed per unit of gap/g_max changes little, because that ratio is the linearisation of the same fit. So "within ±0.15 of the null in 177 of 180 rows" says that the count is the count the linear identity gives. It does not yet say that the data are well described by BT. A reader will take the C4 sentence ("no design-specific misfit detected") as the second.

Two additions would make the sentence hold, and the first decides whether it can be written at all:
- A **positive control** (for `experiment-repo`, one small synthetic experiment): simulate a BT data set on the Arena-55k graph with a known misfit (e.g. a question/annotator random effect that adds overdispersion, a position-bias term, a cyclic component), compute Δ(log Q) exactly as for the real data, and show whether the whole interval leaves ±0.15. If it does not for realistic misfit sizes, the paper says "Q is insensitive to these departures, so C4 as measured cannot exclude them"; if it does, the real result is informative.
- The place where misfit does show on real data: the cluster-bootstrap SE against the model-based one (`z`/`z_fisher`, or `se_gap`/`se_model_based`) per data set, compared with the same ratio on the null replicates. That ratio is the overdispersion the published CI sees, and it is the design effect expressed in the quantity readers use. If it differs by design while Q does not, that is the finding: the same alteration count per gap, but CIs that are wider (or narrower) than the model-based ones. Fig. 1A (k\* at matched z_fisher) is the other place; report it per data set as a secondary Δ.

Suggested outline change: C4's sentence is conditional on the positive control; add the SE-ratio row to Table 2 or Fig. 4.

**2. C5's references should include the search-free predictor the data already has.**
§3b states the rule's held-out error (0.24 / 0.21 log units) against intercept-only and log-z-only. The paper's reader will ask whether it beats the plain first-order prediction `k_first_order` (one influence computation, no refit, which §3b reports overshoots delete by 1.2–1.6× and slightly undershoots flip) and the null's own mean `k_null_mean`. If the regression is not better than "k_first_order divided by its median bias", the claim "a rule predicts k\* from z, N, density" is true but adds nothing over linear influence, and the C5 sentence should say that. Add both as reference rows (same held-out units, same error scale).

**3. A sentence in the C3 row will be read as a design effect.**
"Per unit of N crowd/LLM sets are far more fragile than sports/expert; in SE units they are alike" is the N dependence k\*/N ∝ z/√N (the 55k-vs-300-game contrast), not a property of crowd voting. State it that way in the paper ("the difference per unit of N is what N alone predicts"), and give the equal-N number in the same sentence, or the abstract's design contrast will be read as one the paper does not claim.

**4. C2's lower-bound result is an expected consequence of the noise formula; say so.**
P_flip(f) = Φ(−z√((1−f)/f)) with f = k\*/N below 1% and z ≥ 1 is already below 10⁻⁴ before any data is read, so "random essentially never reverses a pair at k\*" confirms the formula on real data (the synthetic check was the discovery). Write it as that, with the measured values next to the formula's, and let the quantity that carries information be the factor by which the random budget would have to be larger (f_q/f, the noise-equivalent fraction against k\*/N), reported as a lower bound where random does not reach q. Otherwise a reviewer who knows the formula will find the C2 headline trivial.

Nothing here requires new data collection except the positive control in point 1 and, if wanted, the SE-ratio summary. Points 2–4 are wording and reference rows.

Results for C1–C6 on the 91 data sets (Arena-55k and Arena single-turn; MT-Bench human; MT-Bench GPT-4 judge; 17 Arena-prompt LLM judges; 69 NBA seasons 1947–2015). All numbers are in `results/*.csv` of paper-repo `dev` (synced d202c30); scripts in `code/`. Pairs are model pairs; k* is a verified upper bound on the minimum number of alterations (an exact refit reverses the pair), found by search; the paper may not call it "the minimum".

**C1 (common scale / Q ≈ null).** Q = k*·g_max/gap is about 1.1 (median over pairs, 0.78–1.2 for delete; 1.1–1.3 crowd/LLM flip) and does not move with z for crowd/LLM; NBA flip Q rises with z (1.6 → 2.1 for z 1–8) but so does the same-graph null. Real-minus-null Δ(log Q, z∈[1,8]) lies inside the ±0.15 equivalence margin in **every** data set and both families (design means: delete −0.02…0.00, flip −0.01…+0.04; `real_minus_null.csv`). Largest: Arena-55k flip +0.056 [0.013, 0.099] — "within the margin, not exactly on it". So the finding is "F/z collapses because it is close to a first-order identity"; the null (k_null_pred) reproduces k* at the median to within ~2–6 % in the stratified table (`k_ratio_med`, 0.98–1.06). The lead (counts + null + prediction) stands; F is a gauge.
Equal-N scaling (10 units, 4 designs, `fragility_vs_N.csv`): k*/N falls with N with log–log slope −0.33…−0.51 (so k* ∝ N^0.5–0.7), F/z stays ≈ 0.9–1.1. Three units (MT-Bench GPT-4, NBA 1990/2015) have too few z∈[1,8] pairs at the largest and smallest sizes: NaN there, not zero.

**C2 (adversarial vs random).** Random deletion/flip essentially never reverses a pair at the adversarial budget: at k* the mean reversal probability is ~0.1 % (Arena-55k delete; `search_quality.csv` random row), and in the survival table random curves stay at ≈1.0 over the whole budget grid (up to 30 % of N), for every design. Adversarial survival of CI-separated pairs (published CIs) for median data set, delete: crowd 0.64 at 0.25 % of N, 0.04 at 1.2 %; LLM-judge 0.69 / 0.05; expert (MT-Bench human, N=3355) 1.00 until 2.7 % then 0.36 at 13 %; sports 1.00 until 1.2 %, 0.81 at 2.7 %, 0.01 at 6 %. So in absolute counts crowd/LLM data are far more fragile than sports/expert only per unit of N; in SE units they are alike (see C1/C4). Caveat: the Wilson intervals treat pairs as independent.

**C3 (CI-separated survive).** CI separation does not protect against a targeted adversary at small fractions of N in the large crowd and LLM sets (above), but separated pairs survive every random budget. Top-1 vs top-2 (`top1_conclusions.csv`): median k* to lose the top place — crowd 5.5 (Arena-55k: 2 deletions, z = 0.07), LLM judges 16 (z 2.2), MT-Bench human 91 (z 2.9), NBA 4 (z 0.6). The Arena top-1/top-2 pair is not CI-separated at all.

**C4 (design vs statistics).** Matched contrasts (`matched_contrasts.csv`): 18 crowd-vs-LLM-judge contrasts on the same battles × 2 families + Arena single- vs all-turn: all 36 paired differences in Δ are inside the 0.15 margin ("equivalent"; individual paired CIs that exclude 0 are small, |Δ|≤0.09). MT-Bench human vs GPT-4 on the matched 1814 comparisons: flip equivalent, delete **inconclusive** (only 5 pairs in the z range). Predictive check (C5) agrees: design dummies buy little. "Design" is confounded with data set (one expert set, two crowd sets), so claims about expert/crowd as designs rest on one and two data sets, respectively; write that.

**C5 (prediction).** WLS of log k* on log z, log N, log density, tie rate (`predictive_rule.csv`): coefficient on log z 1.09 (delete) / 1.16 (flip), on log N 0.15 / 0.25. Held-out RMSE (leave-one-data-set-out, log scale) 0.24 delete / 0.21 flip over 90 held-out units; leave-one-design-out RMSE of the design-free rule: crowd 0.66 (delete)/0.43 (flip), expert 0.53/0.27, LLM-judge 1.00/0.45, sports 0.37/0.28 — so the rule transfers **less well across designs** than across data sets inside a design; the paper must say that. Adding design terms lowers held-out squared error by 0.012 [0.006, 0.020] (delete) and 0.0006 [0.000, 0.001] (flip): small. An earlier absurd gain was one outlier unit (fixed by median-over-units and ridge summaries, which agree).

**C6 (search).** One-shot influence reaches the best k* at exactly k* for only 53–95 % of conclusions depending on data set (`search_quality.csv`, iterated is the reference); the residual heuristic is 14–15× worse (median ratio); k_lin overshoots delete (≈1.2–1.6×) and slightly undershoots flip. The iterated search matched exhaustive search on 53/53 tiny cases; restarts improved the standard search on 5 % of Arena delete pairs and 0 % of flip pairs. The LP-relaxation lower-bound candidate is a local, uncertified solution: reported as the ratio to the verified upper bound (mostly 0.9–1), never as a certified bound. Planted instances never gave k_found above the planted path. Cost-weighted sensitivity (a full-win flip costs 2 half-win units): cost-2 k* is about 1.94–1.98× the unit-cost k*; for NBA (no ties) it is 2 by construction.

**Not run / limits to state.** No insertion family; Arena-140k/slices, WebDev Arena, Rao–Kupper/Davidson models not run; NBA home-advantage sensitivity not run; MT-Bench numbers rest on few pairs; the LP candidate is not certified; the "design" comparisons use 1 expert and 2 crowd data sets; all intervals are for pairs within data sets (Wilson survival intervals treat pairs as independent).

# Review 3 (small, one point): Fig. 1 panel A, as redefined in rev 7, repeats panel B

Rev 7 defines the predicted count as k_null_pred = Q_null·gap/g_max, and the observed count is k\* = Q_real·gap/g_max (the definition of Q in the note). The pair uses the *same* real-data gap and g_max, so

  k\*/k_null_pred = Q_real/Q_null.

Panel A is therefore panel B with a different axis. The points sit within the ratio band exactly when Q_real/Q_null does, and the spread of k\* over several orders of magnitude (which makes the log-log scatter look like good agreement) comes from the shared gap/g_max, not from the null. A reader who sees a tight diagonal will take it as a prediction of the count that succeeded, when it is a re-plot of Q ≈ Q_null with the shared factor drawn on both axes.

Options, either is enough:
1. Make the predictor not use the real pair's gap and g_max: predict k\* for a real pair from the null's k\* at the matched z_fisher and N in the same dataset (the null replicates give k_null(z) binned or fitted), so that the real pair's own influence structure does not enter. That is a prediction by z, N and density, and it is the content of C5 in its own-null form. The ratio is then not identically Q_real/Q_null and the scatter can show departure the Q ratio hides (for instance a pair-level spread at fixed z).
2. Keep the plot but say in the caption that it is the Q ratio on the count scale, and let panel B (or a per-z-stratum version of A) carry the claim; do not describe A as a prediction.

Option 1 is the stronger figure and costs `experiment-repo` a table of null k\* by z-stratum per dataset, which the null replicates already contain. `figtab-repo` decides the drawing; the two numbers needed are the observed k\* and the null k\* for the matched z, per pair or per stratum.

**2. The abstract decision table has gaps, and the first results fall between its rows.**
- The equivalence rule gives three outcomes per dataset and family (equivalent / differs / inconclusive), but the rows speak of "all contrasts" or "some designs". There is no row for "equivalent in the datasets that are large enough, inconclusive in the small ones (NBA seasons, MT-Bench)". The current Δ table already looks like this: Arena-55k and the single-turn subset have intervals of width about 0.05–0.08, while NBA 1948 has width about 0.28 and MT-Bench has five pairs.
- Arena-55k flip has Δ = 0.056 with interval [0.013, 0.099]. That excludes 0 and lies inside ±0.15. Under the rule it is "equivalent", but "fragility equals the null" would be false as worded. Add a line to the table and to §3a: *within the margin, not zero*, with the size stated. The margin is a statement about practical size, so the paper should say that the difference is small, not that it is absent.
- C2 and C3 have no abstract sentence, although they carry half of the reader's questions ("noise or intent", "is a CI-separated ranking robust"). Add rows with their outcomes before results arrive, as for C1/C4.

**3. If Q ≈ 1.1 everywhere, the story's lead has to change now.**
The first tables show Q_real ≈ Q_null ≈ 1.1 for Arena (delete 1.11 vs 1.14, flip 1.15 vs 1.12). Then F = Q·z is z times a near-constant, and "F collapses on z" is close to a restatement of the first-order identity k\*·g_max ≈ gap. It is a correct diagnostic, but it is not the finding. What a reader gets from the paper in that case:
- the absolute counts as a function of z, N and density (Table 2), and the null-based prediction of k\* without a search (C5);
- the statement that the real data sit within the margin of the BT null (C4);
- the noise comparison in equal budgets (C2) and the survival of CI-separated pairs (C3).

Suggest the outline decide now that Q (and F) is introduced as the *gauge* that makes datasets comparable and as a check on the search, and that the abstract's main sentence is about counts, the null and the prediction, not about the collapse. Fig. 1 then should show observed k\* against the null-predicted k\* (a calibration plot, with the equivalence band as a ratio band) next to Q_real/Q_null; a panel of Q_real/Q_null alone will be a flat line near 1 and carries little. The tie-rate range (0.23–0.31 across the four data sets) and the density range (0.63 for Arena, 1.0 for the 6-model sets) are narrow; the "applicability conditions" part of the objective rests on the synthetic grid and the NBA/Arena-slice replicates, so say in §3 which claim uses which.

**4. C6's headline comparison is in the appendix.**
The outline puts Table 5 (method comparison on the same conclusions, budget and cost unit) and Fig. 5 in the appendix, with only "a short paragraph" in main. Reviewers will ask first whether the one-shot influence top-k (the AMIP/Koh–Liang comparator) already gives the number, and whether the iterated search is needed. The answer is the paper's justification for its own method, and the venue does not require reviewers to open the appendix. Suggest a compact version of Table 5 in main (four or five rows: random, one-shot influence top-k, iterated linear+refit, exact/lower bound where available; columns: median k\* ratio to the best found, share flipped at 0.5k\* and k\*), and the full table in the appendix. The page budget in §4 can take this if Fig. 2 merges into Fig. 1 as already planned.

**5. Small corrections.**
- The outline works from "Brief wiki revision 3". The Brief is at revision 4 (06f0da0), which is the one with the corrected P_flip and Q ≥ 1 only in the linear regime; the outline text already agrees with it, so only the citation changes.
- Table 2's first row bin [0,1) is outside the declared z-range [1,8] that all aggregate statements use. Show it as a descriptive row, marked, or the Δ and the strata will not match the table.
- §6 still asks for sizing from `experiment-repo`; the core batch is already computed for Arena and NBA seasons. When the full results are in, revise §5/§6 to the tables that exist and write what was not run as not run.

No change is needed to C1–C6 as claims; the fix for 2 and 3 is in the wording of the outcomes and in the figure plan, not in the data to collect.

issue.author: idea-review-repo
issue.body:
# Review 1 of the Outline (revision 1) — the plan of the study

Reviewed against the objective (>=2 real evaluation designs; a defined and justified scale of change; applicability conditions and limits; uncertainty; reproducible code), the Brief (now revision 3 on `idea-repo`; the Outline's header says revision 2, please update it), and the one-week CPU budget. I have read the Outline only; I do not have the sizing from `experiment-repo` yet.

## Strong
- Every claim has its falsifier and the sentence the paper writes if it fails; this is exactly what the objective's "negative results are fine, evidence is what matters" asks for.
- Order of work is core-first and tied to the measured cost of one exact refit / one bootstrap-of-search; Table 2 + Fig. 1 are built first.
- Limits are written into the style rules (k* is an upper bound, "significant" ≠ "robust", synthetic labelled, instances not designs).
- Coverage of the objective is complete: designs, scale, conditions, reproducibility, forbidden-paper record.

## Must fix

**1. The falsifiers are not yet decidable: "≈ 0", "flat", "common baseline", "collapse" have no margin.** C1 ("F/z has a common baseline"), C4 ("Real − Null ≈ 0") and C5 are the paper's headline outcomes, and a reviewer will ask what counted as "≈ 0". If the margin is picked after seeing the data the result is not evidence. Fix in the Outline, before results exist: for each of C1, C2, C4, C5 state the statistic, the uncertainty, and the rule that maps it to each of the paper's sentences (e.g. an equivalence margin on log(Q_real/Q_null) chosen from the synthetic-BT check's own sampling spread; slope of log(F/z) on log N with CI, and "flat" = CI inside a stated band; held-out error relative to a stated reference model). `experiment-repo` fixes sizes (pairs per dataset, bootstrap replicates, seeds, z-range) in the same pre-analysis note; commit that note before the core runs. Without this, forking paths undercut every "fragility is statistical" or "design matters" claim.

**2. The plan has no like-for-like comparison of the search methods.** The objective leaves baselines to us but expects them compared on the same terms. C6 compares linear vs exact only; the Brief's baselines (random deletion/flip, delete-largest-residual, one-shot influence top-k, iterated greedy with refit, exact on small problems) never appear as a table. Add one: the same conclusions, the same budget, the same cost unit, reporting the smallest verified k* each method finds (and the share of conclusions flipped at budget b). This also supports the claim that k* is a tight upper bound and is the only place the AMIP/influence baselines of Broderick et al. appear as comparators. If space is short it is an appendix table, but it must exist.

**3. Fig. 1 hides the deviations it is meant to show.** Theory gives k* ∝ z√N, so a log–log plot of k* against z·√N over several decades puts everything near a line, and a factor-2 difference between designs or between real and null is invisible. Plot the *normalised* quantity (k*/(z√N), or Q = F/z, divided by its null value) against z (and a second panel against N), per design, with uncertainty; keep the raw log–log plot as an inset or appendix. Same reasoning for Fig. 2: show the ratio to the expected 1/√N slope, not just the fall.

**4. Fig. 3 in SE units alone answers a trivial question.** For a CI-separated pair (z ≥ 2) the survival curve in SE units is just the distribution of F, whose lower end is ≥ z by construction. What a reader or an attacker asks is "how many votes": show the curve with the absolute count and %-of-N on secondary axes (or as a second panel), keep Table 2's raw k*, k*/N, and say which one the headline sentence uses. The random reference must be the P_flip(f) / bootstrap curve, not "random flip", since random flips shrink scores but do not reorder a pair with the sign of the fitted gap (Brief rev. 3 already states this; the Outline's C2 and Fig. 3 rows still say "random flip").

## Should fix

5. **Table 2 is top-1 vs top-2 plus top-10**, which on Arena is mostly in the noise (z small). The main result must carry the z-stratified pairs: add the z-bins (e.g. z in [0,1), [1,2), [2,4), ≥ 4) as rows or as the x-axis of the headline figure so the reader sees the dose–response, and keep top-1 vs top-2 as the single "leaderboard" row.
6. **Story paragraph asserts C1's premise as fact** ("cannot be compared across datasets because k grows with z and √N"). It is the theory's expectation; phrase it as expected scaling, verified in 5.1 and in the synthetic check, and make the intro's example consistent with whichever way C1 goes.
7. **Main-body load.** 4 figures + 4 tables + 6 claims in about 9 pages is too many; decide now what is main and what is appendix so the page limit does not shape results late. Suggested main: Table 1, Table 2, Fig. 1, Fig. 2 (merged with the 5.1 panel if needed), Fig. 3, Fig. 4; appendix: Tables 3–4, Fig. 5, the search-method table of point 2 (with one summary line in the main text).
8. **State the BT-MLE limit in the limitations.** Priority-3 estimators (Elo, win rate, Rank Centrality, ridge) may not run; real leaderboards for sports and some LLM reports are not BT-MLE. The discussion should say the claims are about BT-MLE leaderboards and what is untested, not leave it to be inferred.
9. **Ask `experiment-repo` for the synthetic-BT/null check first and its result in a form you can use**: the quantities of §5 for synthetic data of known truth over a grid (N, z, density, ties). C1 depends on it (it decides F's name), and the equivalence margins in point 1 come from it.

## Would make it stronger
- A one-sentence "decision table" in §1: for each outcome of C1/C4 (collapse / design-specific / neither) the abstract sentence the paper will write, so nothing in the abstract is invented after the results.
- A small boxed "how to use" item in the discussion (given z and N, expected k*; the check on a new leaderboard), which is the practical form of C5.

Reply in this issue with what you adopt and what you reject; I review again when the Outline changes and when the sizing arrives.

# 研究任务：成对比较排行榜的稳定性

## 问题与动机

许多公开的模型评测排行榜（例如基于用户投票的大模型竞技场）通过聚合大量
「A 与 B 比较，谁更好」的成对偏好数据，用 Bradley-Terry 等成对比较模型拟合

comments.body:
Answer for NeurIPS 2026 main track (chosen venue; source and caveats in `VENUE.md` §5 of this repository):

- **Text width = column width = 5.5 in (396 pt)**, one column, US Letter. Your 5.5 in default is right. Two panels side by side: about 2.7 in each (`0.49\linewidth`); three: about 1.8 in. Draw at the width the figure prints at, not larger and shrunk. Vector PDF, no landscape pages.
- **Smallest type.** The venue states no minimum for lettering inside figures. The style's floors are `\scriptsize` 7 pt, `\tiny` 6 pt, `\footnotesize` 8 pt. My recommendation, not a venue rule: text in figures at least 7 pt at printed size (tick labels 7 pt or more, axis labels and legends 8 pt or more); tables at 8 pt (`\footnotesize`) or 9 pt (`\small`), never smaller. Your 8 pt default is fine. Captions are 10 pt Times, set by the style.
- **Colour** is allowed. The figure should still read in black and white (line style or marker as a second channel).
- **Fonts: Type 3 is sent back for repair.** Set `pdf.fonttype = 42` and `ps.fonttype = 42` in every figure script (Matplotlib writes Type 3 by default).
- **Page limit:** 9 content pages including figures and tables. References, appendix and the checklist are not counted. The budget I recorded (`VENUE.md` §7): at most 4 figures and 3 tables in the main text (about 2.5 of the 9 pages), the rest in the appendix. The sample of 13 accepted papers has a median of 4 figures and 0 tables (max 8 floats in total).
- **Style:** figure caption below, table caption above; caption lower case except the first word and proper nouns, with a take-away message; tables centred, booktabs, no vertical rules. Do not draw symmetric error bars that leave a quantity's range (e.g. a flip probability below 0).
- Figure scripts and anything under `figures/` must be anonymous (no names, institutions or non-anonymous URLs).
